newsitem.title: BRAZIL: GN unveils $1.25 billion Brazil expansion.
newsitem.headline: GN unveils $1.25 billion Brazil expansion.

text.p: General Motors Corp. announced plans Monday to invest $1.25 billion in three new plants in Brazil, one of the world's fastest-growing automobile markets and a springboard for other South American nations.

"Brazil is on its way to becoming a power in vehicle production with all the conditions to become one of the world's top five producers," said Mark Hogan, president of GM's Brazilian subsidiary General Motors do Brasil (GMB).

GMB said it would build a $600 million assembly plant to produce an annual 100,000 vehicles from its Chevrolet line in an as-yet-undisclosed location in Brazil's southernmost state of Rio Grande do Sul.
A $500 million component plant will be located in Santa Catarina state, also in Brazil's south, while $150 million will be invested in a unit in southeastern Sao Paulo state to produce body parts.
Local suppliers will provide 40 percent of the investment which should be completed by 1999 and takes GM's total investment in Brazil to $3.5 billion.

GMB said the location of its plants would facilitate transportation of its vehicles throughout the Mercosur customs union, which comprises Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay, and to Chile which is associated with the trade bloc.
Further investments may be announced soon in Brazil's northeast and north with a view to supplying that region of Brazil and countries such as Venezuela, officials said.

Brazilian automobile sales have soared from about 1 million units in 1992 to an expected 1.8 million this year, thanks mainly to a new climate of low inflation and the emergence of once non-existent consumer credit.
GM's announcement on Monday came on the heels of similar expansion plans by Volkswagen, Ford and Fiat, its traditional rivals in Brazil.
Renault, Toyota, Mercedes Benz and Asia Motors are among newcomers also setting up new plants, taking expected auto investment in Brazil to about $19 billion between now and the year 2000.

GMB officials said their latest plans would not have been viable without Brazil's controversial Car Industry Regime which allows companies that manufacture locally and observe a 60 percent national content rule to import under a 35 percent import tariff, half the normal charge.

"We are growing to be competitive in Mercosur and in Brazil. The regime is vital for that," GMB Vice President Andre Beer told reporters. "It's our guiding light that lets us see the future and plan ahead."

Beer said the regime was key to the auto industry in Brazil while reforms, including a shake-up of the tax system, and privatisation of the country's ports and infrastructure remained on the drawing board.
Brazil's auto rules have been challenged by the United States, Japan, South Korea and other nations at the World Trade Organisation (WTO) where formal consultations are ongoing.

"There were those who said the regime would fall apart after the first WTO meeting," beamed Brazilian Industry and Commerce Minister Francisco Dornelles, one of the regime's staunchest defenders. "Everything is blue skies."
